name: Fleetwood
title: Fleetwood Hull Gauging | UTM for Coasters and Fishing Vessels
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at Fleetwood for coasters, fishing vessels, dredgers and workboats on the Wyre: hull, deck, tanks and piping gauged alongside.
h1: Thickness Measurement for Small Ships and Fishing Vessels at Fleetwood
intro: Fleetwood sits at the mouth of the River Wyre on the Lancashire coast, a port that made its name in deep-sea fishing and later ran ferries to Northern Ireland. Today its traffic is smaller: fishing vessels, coasters, workboats and dredgers using tidal quays and a dock entered around high water. Gauging here suits small ships that need hull, deck and tank readings without a long passage to a bigger port. Technicians are sent from India for each job and join the vessel wherever she lies on the Wyre.

highlights.h: A fishing port with a long history
highlights.p: Fleetwood's trawlers once worked the distant grounds off Iceland, and the port still has a fish market and a working fishing harbour. Fishing vessels are hard on steel, and readings on hull, fish hold and deck help owners plan maintenance between seasons.

The enclosed dock is reached through gates that open around high water, and the river berths on the Wyre are fully tidal. Arrivals and departures follow the tide table, so each job is planned around the hours a vessel is afloat and settled at her berth.

Associated British Ports agreed in 2024 to sell the port to Fox Group, which has said it wants to keep Fleetwood working as a cargo port and to move more aggregates by sea. More coaster calls would mean more chances for gauging alongside.

port.h: Fleetwood: a tidal port at the mouth of the Wyre
p: Fleetwood stands at the tip of the Fylde peninsula, on the west bank of the River Wyre where the river opens into Morecambe Bay, with Blackpool a few miles to the south and Knott End directly across the water. It was laid out as a planned town and port in the nineteenth century, and the railway made it a terminus for steamers to Ireland and Scotland and, for decades, one of Britain's busiest fishing ports. The approach channel runs between sands that dry at low water, so ships navigate the Wyre on the tide, keeping to the buoyed and lit channel. Morecambe Bay has a large tidal range, and the river's streams run strongly on both flood and ebb, which is why most vessel movements are timed close to high water and why the harbour's pilots and boatmen matter here.

The traffic has changed more than once. Stena Line's ro-ro service to Larne ended in 2010, and the distant-water fleet that once filled the docks has long gone. What remains is a fishing harbour used by inshore and visiting vessels, a fish market that handles fish landed elsewhere as well as local catches, a marina in the former Wyre Dock, and quays used by coasters, dredgers and workboats. In 2024 Associated British Ports agreed to sell the port to Fox Group, a business with interests in aggregates and transport, which has said it wants to keep Fleetwood handling cargo. If more aggregates move by sea, small bulk coasters will become a more regular sight on the Wyre, and with them the routine hull and hold work that cargo ships need.

Gauging at Fleetwood is therefore small-ship work. Fishing vessels come in between trips or for a maintenance period, coasters arrive and sail on the tide, and dredgers and workboats lie alongside between contracts. None of these vessels carries the elaborate TM plan of a large bulk carrier, but their owners still need to know the condition of shell plating, fish holds, decks, tanks and piping, especially before a survey, a sale or a major repair. Seasonal patterns matter as well: fishing effort follows quotas and weather, and winter gales from the west can keep small vessels in port for days at a time, which is often exactly when an owner can spare the vessel for a few days of inspection without losing earnings.

facilities.h: Where gauging is practical at Fleetwood
p: Fishing vessels and workboats lying alongside in the dock or at the fishing harbour are the simplest jobs. The team gauges shell plating from inside where it is reachable, fish-hold and deck structure, tank boundaries and sea-water piping, and uses magnetic particle inspection on gantries, winch foundations and A-frames where cracking is suspected. On a coaster loading or discharging aggregates, holds are measured as they empty, and ballast tanks are entered once the crew has ventilated them and issued an entry permit.

Fleetwood is not equipped to drydock seagoing merchant ships, so a renewal survey with the hull out of the water is normally carried out at a yard elsewhere, on the Mersey, in Northern Ireland or in Scotland, depending on size and yard availability. For a coaster or dredger the realistic Fleetwood job is condition gauging alongside, timed to the tide and to the vessel's own programme, and used to prepare the steel list for that next docking. A vessel laid up in the dock for a quiet season gives the longest window of all, with time to open and ventilate every tank in turn.
list: Fishing harbour quays — hull, fish-hold, deck and piping gauging on trawlers and other fishing vessels between trips.
Berths inside the dock gates — longer condition surveys on workboats, dredgers and small ships laid up for a season.
Cargo quays — hold, hatch coaming and ballast tank gauging on aggregate coasters during discharge.
River berths on the Wyre — short scopes timed to the hours the vessel is afloat.
Deck machinery — MPI and dye penetrant checks on gantries, winches and A-frames where crews report cracking.

context.h: Rules for fishing vessels and small ships at Fleetwood
p: Many vessels at Fleetwood sit outside the big-ship survey regime. UK fishing vessels are surveyed under codes administered by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, with requirements that depend on length, and only some larger fishing vessels are classed. Owners of smaller vessels still face structural questions at survey, after a grounding, or when buying and selling, and thickness readings give them evidence that a surveyor or a buyer can rely on. Coasters and dredgers that are classed follow the normal class survey cycle, and their owners use gauging in the same way as larger operators do.

Foreign-flagged coasters calling at Fleetwood are subject to port state control by the Maritime and Coastguard Agency under the Paris MoU, and visiting ships are expected to carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under Britain's retained ship recycling rules. Small, older coasters attract inspections because of their age and the short-sea trades they work. Fishing remains a seasonal business, so maintenance and inspection tend to be packed into the quieter months, and an owner who books gauging early can line it up with a planned lay-up rather than giving up fishing days.

jobs.p: Jobs at Fleetwood are small but varied. A fishing vessel owner wants to know whether wasted shell plating near the waterline or around the fish hold needs renewing before the next season; a dredger operator needs tank and hull readings ahead of a class survey; a buyer wants an independent condition check on a workboat before purchase. Each job is planned around the tide and the vessel's availability, with the scope agreed in advance so the team can finish within the time the vessel is in port. Because these vessels rarely have formal TM plans, we prepare a simple sketch-based plan with the owner first, so the readings can be repeated at the next inspection.
list: Hull, fish-hold and deck gauging on a trawler during a maintenance period between fishing trips.
Hopper and tank gauging on a dredger ahead of a class intermediate survey.
Pre-purchase condition survey of a workboat or multicat lying alongside in the dock.
Hold and ballast tank readings on an aggregate coaster while she discharges.
MPI on a trawl gantry, winch seats or crane foundations after the crew reports cracking.

logistics: Manchester Airport is the usual gateway, followed by rail to Blackpool North or Poulton-le-Fylde and a short road journey, or the coastal tramway, to Fleetwood. Flights from India usually connect there through a European or Gulf hub. The team travels on UK visas, so a first visit needs some weeks of notice. Access to the quays is arranged through the vessel's owner or agent, and because movements depend on the tide, the agent confirms the berth and the hours the vessel will be afloat before the team travels.

faqs.q: Do you gauge fishing vessels at Fleetwood?
faqs.a: Yes, and they are among the commonest jobs here. We gauge shell plating, fish-hold and deck structure, tank boundaries and sea-water piping, and check gantries and winch foundations for cracks with magnetic particle inspection. Because many fishing vessels have no formal TM plan, we agree a simple sketch with the owner first, so that readings can be repeated and compared at later inspections.

faqs.q: Can a vessel be gauged at a tidal berth on the Wyre?
faqs.a: Yes, within the hours she is afloat and settled. At a tidal river berth a vessel may take the ground at low water or move with the tide, which affects safe access and some measurements. We plan the scope against the tide table, do tank and internal work first, and leave anything that depends on the vessel's position for when she is afloat at a steady level.

faqs.q: Where do vessels from Fleetwood go for drydocking?
faqs.a: Larger vessels usually go to a yard on the Mersey, in Northern Ireland or in Scotland, depending on size and when a berth is free. We gauge at Fleetwood beforehand, so the owner can send the yard a steel list and plan the docking around known renewals rather than around discoveries made once the vessel is out of the water.

faqs.q: Is it worth gauging a small coaster during a short aggregates call?
faqs.a: Often it is. A coaster discharging aggregates is alongside for a tide or two, and her holds become accessible as cargo comes out. A focused scope on hold frames, tank top, hatch coamings and one or two ballast tanks fits that window, and repeat calls let the owner build up a full picture of the ship over several visits.
